newsitem.title: UK: UK shares end slightly higher but funds stay away.
newsitem.headline: UK shares end slightly higher but funds stay away.

text.p: UK blue chips ended a lethargic session slightly higher on Thursday as institutional investors continued to steer clear of a market currently plagued by a host of uncertainties.
"It's been another nothing day. The funds are just sitting on their cash," the head of trading at a large brokerage said.
"We need some good news to break us out of this stupor but I can't see anything at the moment that will bring back the buyers."
The FTSE 100 index ended 4.3 points higher to 4,298.9 after trading in a narrow 20-point range during the session.

Institutional investors have been conspicuous by their absence so far this week - a period which has seen the Dow Industrials average claw back over 40 percent of the 700 points it had lost since peaking in mid-March.
The Dow Industrials Average was up 14 points by the 1530 GMT London close.

Political as well as economic uncertainties continued to weigh on market sentiment and many fund managers are expected to refrain from aggressive buying until after the May 1 British election, which the opposition Labour party is the odds on favourite to win, dealers said.
"If the polls are right, Labour could have a huge majority and that has frightened a few people away," the head of trading at a major investment bank said.
"Some people fear a Labour government with a big majority might be tempted to do things like raise corporate taxes more aggressively than if it had only a modest majority."

Labour, which is currently leading the ruling Conservatives by around 20 percentage points in the most recent opinion polls, is pledged to place a windfall tax on utilities but some strategists think they may not stop there.

Richard Kersley, strategist at broker BZW fears Labour may be forced to raise up to five billion stg in additional revenues through corporate tax adjustments in order to plug a 10 billion stg hole in Britain's "fragile" finances.
The strong pound, which is trading at near five year highs against major European currencies, is also causing investors a few headaches.
On Wednesday, Reed International Plc and Reuters Holdings Plc became the latest in a growing list of UK corporates who have warned profits growth has been inhibited by sterling's strength.
Sterling was trading at 2.81 marks by 1530 GMT, near its best level against the German currency since October 1992 when the British unit was forced out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Technical analysts said the FTSE may attempt to push up towards 4,330 to 4,335 in the near-term but will probably fail to make much headway beyond that resistance level.
Near-term support is pegged at 4,270.

B.A.T Industries Plc was the most active blue chip, dipping 4-1/2p to 536-1/2 on profit-taking after jumping 28p on Wednesday following news that two U.S. tobacco companies had entered secret negotiations with U.S. plaintiffs in an effort to find an settlement to the industry's legal woes.
LucasVarity Plc was the second most active FTSE 100 constituent, down 3-1/2p to 193 after the company confirmed it had bought back 10 million of its own shares for cancellation.
LucasVarity's share price has been under pressure in recent months amid market concerns about how it would reward investors, 60 percent of whom are in Britain and 40 percent in the U.S.
The share price dip on Thursday reflected the disappointment by British investors who are used to dividend growth as opposed to buy-backs, analysts said.
Standard Chartered Plc gained 18-1/2p to 865-1/2 after Schroders Securities upgraded the stock to a "strong buy" from a "buy".
In a review of the UK banking sector, Schroders also upgraded Lloyds TSB Group Plc, up 5-1/2p to 519-1/2p and cut its rating on National Westminster Bank Plc, down 6-1/2p to 669-1/2.
--Dale Faulken, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
